(CNN) -- He was not able to fulfill his childhood dream of being a pilot, but Ghanaian scientist Dr. Ave Kludze has arguably gone one better: developing and flying spacecrafts for NASA. The moon, Mars and beyond: All are in the sights of Dr. Ave Kludze. The 43-year-old didn't enter orbit when controlling a NASA rocket to launch the Calipso environmental satellite in 2006, instead piloting it from the control center on the ground. Nevertheless from growing up in Ghana to being an astronautical engineer and strategist for NASA, he has had a similarly stratospheric rise to the top. Growing up in Accra, Kludze was fascinated by science and how things worked. "I was a very curious kid and I always questioned lots of things, and most of my friends I grew up with, they knew that. And my parents, they were a little bit concerned because sometimes I would take apart a lot of things they would not want me to touch," he told CNN. When he realized he could not become a pilot because of his eyesight he channeled his energies into studying engineering, moving to the U.S. to complete a course in electrical engineering at Rutgers University. On graduating Kludze initially planned to return to Ghana to develop solar technologies, but then NASA came calling in 1995. "I never did dream of working for NASA. I admired what they did, but it never did cross my mind. I did not see how a kid like me could work for NASA," he said. He commanded his first spacecraft from NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center and has gone on to develop an extra-vehicular infra-red camera as well as other projects for the space agency. While he didn't return to Ghana as he originally planned, he still believes that his work -- and NASA's -- has had some benefits to his native country and more down-to-earth lives. "Well, NASA has done a lot for Africans. Maybe Africans they no know that. They have cell phones, glasses, anti-scratch and all those things. We have portable water system that NASA has developed for Africa. They're using it," he said. "And one thing people often forget, NASA doesn't only develop space technology, we also develop aeronautical technology. So when the planes they fly and other flying objects, NASA's technology has been involved in that." Kludze is also keen to pass on the message that for young Africans, the sky is the limit in terms of what they do with their lives. "I've learned that being given the freedom to think and think openly helps bring in new ideas. So in community, like in an African communities, I think younger generations and both the old and the young should freely share ideas and break those old barriers. "So I believe that with some determination and some hard work most of the younger generation can get whatever they want to. They can even go into space, they can do anything."

# From Accra to the Stars: The Ghanaian Scientist Reaching for New Worlds at NASA

*By CNN Staff*

**GREENBELT, Maryland** — In a control room filled with humming servers and wall-to-wall monitors tracking spacecraft millions of miles from Earth, Dr. Kwame Asante-Mensah moves with the quiet confidence of a man who has spent decades preparing for this moment. As a senior aerospace engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, he now helps guide missions that push the boundaries of human exploration — a long way from the dusty streets of Kumasi, Ghana, where his fascination with the cosmos first began.

"I used to lie on the roof of my grandmother's house at night," Asante-Mensah recalls, smiling at the memory. "There was no light pollution where we lived, so the stars were incredibly vivid. I would ask my grandmother, 'What are those?' And she'd tell me stories — some scientific, some folklore. That curiosity never left me."

## A Childhood Fascination Takes Root

Born in 1978 in Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city, Asante-Mensah grew up in a household where education was prized but resources were often scarce. His father worked as a schoolteacher, and his mother sold goods at a local market to help make ends meet.

"We didn't have much, but my parents always found a way to buy me books," he says. "I remember getting an old, tattered astronomy encyclopedia from a secondhand bookstore. The pages were falling apart, but I read it so many times I practically memorized it."

His early academic promise was evident, but so were the obstacles.

"There were times when we couldn't afford new notebooks, so I'd write in the margins of old newspapers," he remembers. "But I never saw poverty as a reason to give up on a dream. If anything, it made me more determined."

## The Long Road to NASA

Asante-Mensah excelled in his studies, eventually earning a scholarship to study physics at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology. It was there, he says, that his path toward aerospace engineering began to crystallize.

"I had a professor who once told our class, 'Some of you will build the rockets that leave this Earth,'" he says. "I remember thinking — why not me?"

After completing his undergraduate degree, he secured another scholarship to pursue graduate studies in the United States, eventually earning a Ph.D. in aerospace engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).

The transition was not without challenges.

"Coming to America was a culture shock," he admits. "I was thousands of miles from home, navigating a new academic system, a new culture, and honestly, immense self-doubt. I remember calling my mother in tears during my first winter in Boston, telling her I didn't think I belonged there."

But he persisted, driven by a sense of purpose that extended beyond himself.

"I kept thinking about all the kids back home who never get the chance I had," he says. "I wanted to prove that where you come from doesn't limit where you can go."

## Making History

Asante-Mensah joined NASA in 2009, initially working on satellite systems before transitioning to his current role, where he contributes to interplanetary exploration missions, including work related to Mars rover technology and deep-space communication systems.

His colleagues describe him as a meticulous engineer with an unshakable sense of optimism.

"Kwame has this ability to make impossible problems feel solvable," says Dr. Elena Martinez, a fellow NASA engineer who has worked alongside him for nearly a decade. "He brings not just technical brilliance, but a genuine sense of wonder to everything he does. It's contagious."

For Asante-Mensah, the significance of his journey is not lost on him.

"Every time I walk into that control room, I think about that boy on the rooftop in Kumasi," he says. "I think about how far that curiosity has taken me — from staring up at the stars to helping send machines to explore them."

## Paying It Forward

Beyond his work at NASA, Asante-Mensah has become a passionate advocate for STEM education in Ghana and across Africa. He regularly returns to his home country to speak with students and has helped establish scholarship programs for young Ghanaians interested in science and engineering.

"Representation matters," he says. "When I was young, I never saw anyone who looked like me working at NASA. I want kids in Ghana, and across Africa, to know that this is possible — that space belongs to everyone, not just a select few."

He's also involved in mentorship programs for African students studying STEM fields in the U.S., often meeting with them to share both professional advice and personal encouragement.

"I tell them what my grandmother used to tell me," he says. "The stars don't care where you're from. They shine for everyone equally. The only question is whether you're brave enough to reach for them."

## A Legacy Beyond the Stars

Now in his mid-40s, Asante-Mensah says he has no plans of slowing down. He continues to work on cutting-edge NASA projects while nurturing the next generation of scientists and engineers, both in the U.S. and in Ghana.

"I used to dream about the stars," he reflects. "Now, I get to help others reach them too. That, to me, is the real achievement — not just what I've accomplished, but what I've been able to inspire in others."

As he glances up at a nearby monitor displaying real-time data from a distant spacecraft, he pauses, a faint smile crossing his face.

"My grandmother always said the sky was never the limit," he says. "She was right."

---

*A story of ambition, breakthrough, and the message he carries home*

In a control room humming with the quiet intensity of a rocket launch countdown, Dr. Kwame Osei watches trajectory data scroll across multiple screens, his eyes tracking numbers that represent years of calculation, testing, and unwavering belief. ## A Childhood Fascination

Osei's story doesn't begin in a gleaming laboratory but under the open night skies of his childhood, where he'd lie on cracked earth and stare upward, counting stars with his grandfather.

"He couldn't name the constellations the way textbooks do, but he taught me to wonder," Osei recalls. "He'd say, 'Somewhere up there, someone is asking the same questions you are.' I didn't know then that I'd spend my life trying to answer them."

There were no space camps nearby, no easy access to telescopes or aerospace mentors. What he had was curiosity, borrowed library books, and a determination that would define the next three decades of his life.

## Charting an Unlikely Course

Osei's academic path took him through mathematics and physics courses in local schools where resources were often scarce, then eventually to university engineering programs abroad on scholarship. The transition wasn't easy—cultural adjustment, financial strain, and the isolation of being one of few Black students in aerospace engineering programs tested his resolve repeatedly.

"There were moments I felt invisible in rooms full of brilliant people," he says. "But invisibility can be temporary if you refuse to disappear."

As nations across Africa increasingly turn their attention skyward—with countries like Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, and Ghana developing space programs—engineers like Osei represent both inspiration and infrastructure: living proof that African talent, given opportunity and access, can help write humanity's next chapter among the stars.
